question: Puerto Rico is now seated with a generated legislature rather than nothing, so the question is no longer whether it is covered but whether the numbers are its own. From the Constitution of the Commonwealth of Puerto Rico and its election law: how many members sit in the Senate and in the House of Representatives, including the at-large and district split and any provision that adds members to correct a supermajority; what is the minimum age to stand for each chamber; what residence is required, in the Commonwealth and in the district, and for how long before filing; how long is a term for each chamber; and what is the Governor's term, minimum age and residence requirement? The same for the Resident Commissioner if it is cheap to include. Citations to the article and section, in the instrument's own words, are what we need rather than a summary.

title: Puerto Rico's own legislature and who may stand for it
usableAnswer: One row per office - Senate, House of Representatives, Governor - giving seat count where it applies, minimum age, residence requirement with its duration and whether it is Commonwealth-wide or district, and term length. Each value cited to the constitutional article and section or the statute, quoted closely enough that we can record the instrument's own words. Where a rule has a condition our single-value shape cannot hold, say so plainly rather than flattening it; we would rather record a declared gap than a convenient number.
whyItMatters: Puerto Rico currently plays on drawn numbers. The pack records a minimum age of 23 drawn from the 21-to-24 spread that MN, MO, NJ and NV enacted, and states in its own note that it is not a claim about this jurisdiction's law. That is the game's rule honestly labelled, and the owner's standing rule is that real law always overrides it. So a read answer here does not need any new mechanism - it replaces a drawn value the moment it lands. Until then a player standing for the Senate of Puerto Rico meets a number no Puerto Rican legislature ever enacted, which is the difference between a jurisdiction the game can claim to cover and one it merely does not refuse.
